newsitem.title: KENYA: Ousted Burundi leader may quit US embassy soon.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Burundi leader may quit US embassy soon.

text.p: Burundi's ousted president may soon quit the U.S. ambassador's residence in the Burundian capital seven months after he fled there, a senior diplomat said on Thursday.
Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, an ethnic Hutu, took refuge at the residence two days before a coup by the Tutsi-dominated army last July removed him from power and installed retired major Pierre Buyoya.

Burundi's regime has found a house in Bujumbura where the ousted president could live, a sticking point in negotiations on his departure from the residence, the diplomat and friends of the ousted leader said.
"The government has found a home for him so one of the main conditions for his release has now been fulfilled," a senior diplomat said by telephone from Bujumbura.
"It is now very much a personal decision how comfortable he feels in the U.S. embassy against how afraid he is of coming out," the diplomat said.
A senior government official said he might leave the embassy by the end of this week.
But Ntibantunganya's party Frodebu, the main legal pro-Hutu opposition, said it opposed his departure from the residence because of the regime's harrassment of leading Frodebu officials.
Authorities released Frodebu secretary-general Augustin Nzogibwani last week from a week's solitary confinment after accusing him of fomenting civil unrest.
"The party isn't in favour of his leaving the embasssy. The same army that wants him out (of the embassy) put him there," said Frederique Bangvunyumvira, Frodebu spokesman.
"If he does leave Frodebu isn't responsible for the consequences," he said.
Frodebu recognizes Buyoya as president and has agreed to work with him, but it remains unclear if Ntibantunganya would renounce his claim to the presidency if he left the embassy.
Ntibantunganya has dropped out of the limelight since July. His wife left Burundi last August.

His departure from the residence would be a major boost for Buyoya's government, isolated by sanctions imposed by East African states demanding unconditional negotiations between the army and Hutu rebels.
The U.N. human rights agency said in January 1,000 civilians had been killed in Burundi since December, almost all by the army.
Frodebu won elections in June 1993 and more than 150,000 people have died since the country's first Frodebu president was murdered in October 1993 in an attempted army coup.
